places.quote: A **Link Function** $g$ is a monotone, differentiable function in a [[Generalized Linear Model]] that connects the **expected value** of the response $\mu = E[Y]$ to the **linear predictor** $\eta = \mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}$:

**Model A.** B fits the training data better ($310$ against $380$) but predicts worse.

The variance inflation factor (VIF) of a regression coefficient measures how much the variance of its estimator is inflated by collinearity with the other predictors, relative to a model in which that predictor is uncorrelated with the others.

places.quote: so $\sigma^2/S_{jj}$ is $\text{Var}(\hat\beta_j)$ when $x_j$ is the only predictor, and $\text{VIF}_j$ is the factor by which the other predictors inflate it

places.quote: so $\sigma^2/S_{jj}$ is $\text{Var}(\hat\beta_j)$ when $x_j$ is the only predictor

requirements.statement: The hat matrix is H = X(X^T X)^{-1} X^T, the matrix that projects the response vector onto the column space of the design matrix.

places.quote: $$\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top$$
projecting $\mathbf{y}$ onto the column space of $\mathbf{X}$

places.quote: $$\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{y}$$
In OLS, each $\hat{y}_i = \sum_j h_{ij}\,y_j$ is a weighted combination of all the responses

requirements.statement: In local regression (loess), the span s is the fraction of the observations used in each local fit, and it controls the smoothness of the fitted curve.

places.quote: Gather the fraction $s = k/n$ of training points whose $x_i$ are closest to $x_0$.

requirements.statement: A larger span in local regression averages over more data points and gives a smoother, less variable fit, while a smaller span follows local fluctuations and gives a wiggly, higher-variance fit.

places.quote: The smaller $s$ is, the more local and wiggly the fit. A very large $s$ gives a global fit that uses all the training observations.
A smaller span makes each fit more local, which gives a wigglier, more flexible curve with more degrees of freedom.

requirements.statement: Knots and the order of the piecewise polynomial are tuning features of splines and piecewise polynomial regression, not of local regression, so changing them does not adjust the smoothness of a local regression fit.

places.quote: A **regression spline** fits separate low-degree polynomials over regions of $X$ separated by **knots**, constrained so that they join smoothly at the knots.
Knots and boundary constraints belong to [[Regression Spline|splines]]; local regression has none to adjust.

requirements.statement: The lasso estimates regression coefficients by minimizing the residual sum of squares plus a penalty equal to lambda times the sum of the absolute values of the coefficients (an L1 penalty).

places.quote: $$\text{Lasso:}\quad \min_{\beta}\ \mathrm{RSS} + \lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}\lvert\beta_j\rvert$$

requirements.statement: As the lasso tuning parameter lambda increases, coefficients shrink toward (and some become exactly) zero, so the model becomes less flexible; lambda = 0 gives the unpenalized least squares fit.

places.quote: $\lambda = 0$ returns least squares; $\lambda \to \infty$ drives every coefficient to zero.
**Lasso** ($\ell_1$) sets some coefficients exactly to zero, so it performs [[Variable Selection]] as part of the fit

requirements.statement: Training MSE decreases as model flexibility increases, so as lambda increases (flexibility decreases) the training MSE rises monotonically from its minimum at lambda = 0.

places.quote: Training error is not a guide — it falls monotonically with complexity.
Training MSE falls every time flexibility is added, because a model with as many free parameters as observations can reproduce them exactly.

requirements.statement: Test MSE is U-shaped as a function of flexibility (or lambda): it first falls as variance is reduced, then rises as bias grows.

places.quote: By the [[Bias-Variance Tradeoff|bias-variance tradeoff]], test error is U-shaped in flexibility: bias falls, variance rises.

Test MSE is U-shaped instead: past the minimum, each added parameter fits errors $\varepsilon_i$ that belong to this sample only and will not recur, so the variance of $\hat{f}$ rises by more than its squared bias falls.

requirements.statement: The first principal component is the linear combination of the variables (direction in variable space) along which the data have maximum variance, i.e., the direction of greatest elongation of the scatter.

places.quote: **First principal component** — the direction $\mathbf{z}_1 = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\phi}_1$ that maximizes $\text{Var}(\mathbf{z}_1)$
The first component is the direction along which the observations vary the most.

requirements.statement: Best subset selection fits all possible models of each size k, picks the best model of each size (highest R-squared), then compares the best models across sizes using a criterion such as AIC.

places.quote: Fit every combination of the $p$ predictors; keep the best model of each size (lowest RSS, or lowest [[Deviance]] for a GLM), then choose among the sizes as in the last row

requirements.statement: Forward stepwise selection starts with the intercept-only model and at each step adds the one predictor that most improves the fit (highest R-squared among models with one more predictor), keeping previously selected predictors, giving one model per size; the final model is chosen across sizes by a criterion such as AIC.

places.quote: Start with no predictors; at each step add the one that most improves the fit; choose among the resulting sizes as in the last row
if the best one-predictor model is $\{x_1\}$ but the best two-predictor model is $\{x_2, x_3\}$, forward stepwise cannot reach it, because every later model must keep $x_1$

requirements.statement: Forward stepwise considers far fewer models than best subset and its path is nested, so it may miss the best model of a given size; best subset's chosen model has AIC no larger than that of forward stepwise.

places.quote: Best subset selection fits all $2^p$ models; forward and backward stepwise each fit only $1 + p(p+1)/2$.

requirements.statement: R-squared never decreases when predictors are added, so it can only be used to compare models with the same number of parameters; AIC is needed to compare models of different sizes.

places.quote: Compare models with different numbers of predictors via [[AIC]] (or $C_p$), [[BIC]], adjusted $R^2$ or [[Cross-Validation]] error — not by raw RSS, $R^2$ or deviance, which always improve as predictors are added

requirements.statement: The probability of at least one occurrence of an event equals 1 minus the probability that it never occurs (complement rule).

places.quote: The complement rule is the workhorse shortcut — "at least one" is almost always faster as $1 - P(\text{none})$.
P(\text{at least one}) &= 1 - P(\text{no claims}) \\

requirements.statement: The probability of a specific path of states in a Markov chain is the product of the successive one-step transition probabilities along the path, by the Markov property.

places.quote: $$P(X_1 = \cdots = X_n = i \mid X_0 = i) = (P_{ii})^{n}$$
Staying healthy throughout has probability $0.85^2 = 0.7225$. The gap $0.7425 - 0.7225 = 0.02$ is the path H $\to$ D $\to$ H, $(0.10)(0.20)$: disabled in year 1, recovered by year 2.

requirements.statement: To find the probability of avoiding a set of states over several steps, sum over all paths that stay outside that set, using only transitions into the non-target states at each step.

requirements.statement: The exponential distribution is memoryless: Pr[T > s + t | T > s] = Pr[T > t], so the remaining time given survival to any age has the same exponential distribution.

places.quote: Its defining property is **memorylessness**: $P(X > s + t \mid X > s) = P(X > t)$, making it the unique continuous distribution with no aging effect
A direct consequence: given $X > d$, the excess $X - d$ is again $\text{Exp}(\theta)$.

requirements.statement: For an exponential random variable with mean θ, the survival function is Pr[T > t] = e^{-t/θ}.

places.quote: Work from the survival function $S(x) = e^{-x/\theta}$ rather than the CDF; almost every exponential question is a tail probability

requirements.statement: To find the probability of exceeding a total time given time already elapsed, apply memorylessness by subtracting the elapsed time from the threshold and computing the unconditional survival probability at the remaining amount.

places.quote: Its defining property is **memorylessness**: $P(X > s + t \mid X > s) = P(X > t)$
A direct consequence: given $X > d$, the excess $X - d$ is again $\text{Exp}(\theta)$.

requirements.statement: Two states of a Markov chain communicate if each is reachable from the other in some finite number of steps (positive n-step transition probability in both directions).

places.quote: State $j$ is *accessible* from $i$ if $P^n_{ij} > 0$ for some $n \geq 0$, and $i$ and $j$ *communicate* ($i \leftrightarrow j$) if each is accessible from the other.

requirements.statement: A class of a Markov chain is an equivalence class of mutually communicating states; the state space is partitioned into classes, and a state that does not return to itself still forms its own class.

places.quote: Communication is an equivalence relation, so it splits the states into **classes**; the chain is **irreducible** if there is only one. Every state communicates with itself ($P^0_{ii} = 1$), so a state that nothing leads back to is a class on its own.

requirements.statement: To find the classes, read the transition matrix for which states can be reached from each state (positive entries, including via multi-step paths), then group states that are mutually reachable and count the groups.

places.quote: Read the one-step moves off the nonzero entries: $1 \to \{1, 2\}$, $2 \to \{1, 2\}$, $3 \to \{1, 2\}$, $4 \to \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$, $5 \to \{5\}$.

requirements.statement: A state i is absorbing if P_ii = 1, so the chain never leaves it; an absorbing state forms a class by itself.

places.quote: An **absorbing** state has $P_{ii} = 1$ — death in a [[Multi-State Model]], default in [[Credit Rating Migration]].

requirements.statement: A state that cannot be re-entered after leaving it (no path back to it) is transient and forms a singleton class.

places.quote: State 3 leads to 1 and 2, but nothing leads back to it — only state 4 enters 3, and 3 cannot reach 4. So $\{3\}$ is a class by itself, transient, with $f_3 = 0$.

requirements.statement: The limiting (stationary) distribution of a Markov chain is a probability vector pi satisfying pi P = pi with entries summing to 1; for an irreducible aperiodic chain it equals the limiting probabilities.
requirements.concept: Stationary Distribution of a Markov Chain

places.quote: A **stationary distribution** $\boldsymbol{\pi}$ satisfies $\boldsymbol{\pi}P = \boldsymbol{\pi}$ with $\sum_i \pi_i = 1$; for an irreducible aperiodic chain it is the long-run fraction of time spent in each state

The **Stationary Distribution** $\boldsymbol{\pi}$ of a [[Markov Chain]] is a probability vector that one transition leaves unchanged: a chain started in $\boldsymbol{\pi}$ stays in $\boldsymbol{\pi}$.

requirements.statement: Each row of a transition probability matrix sums to 1 because from any state the chain must move to some state.

places.quote: $$\sum_{j} P_{ij} = 1 \quad \text{for every row } i$$
$P_{ij} \geq 0$ is the probability of moving from state $i$ to state $j$ in one step; each row sums to 1

requirements.statement: If the stationary distribution is uniform over all states, then every column of the transition matrix sums to 1 (the matrix is doubly stochastic), and conversely.

places.quote: A matrix whose columns also sum to one is *doubly stochastic*. For a chain with finitely many states the uniform distribution is then stationary, and it is the chain's unique [[Stationary Distribution|stationary distribution]] when the chain is irreducible.
Each column also sums to 1, so the uniform distribution is stationary: $\pi_S = \pi_F = \pi_H = \tfrac13$.

requirements.statement: Find unknown transition probabilities by combining row-sum constraints (each row sums to 1) with the column-sum constraints implied by the stationary condition pi P = pi.
requirements.concept: Stationary Distribution of a Markov Chain

places.quote: $$\pi_j = \sum_i \pi_i\, P_{ij} \quad \text{for every } j$$
A doubly stochastic matrix has a uniform $\boldsymbol{\pi}$.
A matrix whose columns also sum to one is *doubly stochastic*.

requirements.statement: The net level annual premium for a fully discrete unit whole life insurance issued at age x is P_x = A_x / ä_x, the whole life APV divided by the life annuity-due APV (equivalence principle).
requirements.concept: Net Level Premium for Whole Life Insurance

places.quote: $$P = \frac{A_x}{\ddot{a}_x}$$
a premium $P$ paid at the start of each year while $(x)$ is alive is a [[Life Annuity|life-annuity-due]], so $A_x = P\,\ddot{a}_x$
Setting $E[L_0]=0$ gives $P = S\,A_x/\ddot{a}_x$.

requirements.statement: A_x is the actuarial present value of a unit whole life insurance paying at the end of the year of death, and ä_x is the actuarial present value of a life annuity-due paying 1 at the start of each year while the person is alive.
requirements.concept: Whole Life Insurance and Life Annuity-Due APVs

places.quote: In the life-table model of Exam MAS-I the benefit is paid at the **end of the year of death**, and its actuarial present value (the **net single premium**) for a life aged $x$ is $A_x$.
A **life-annuity-due** pays 1 at the start of each year while $(x)$ is alive; its actuarial present value (EPV) is $\ddot{a}_x$.

requirements.statement: Read A_x and ä_x for a given age from the Illustrative Life Table (at 6% interest) and compute each premium from them before taking the difference.

places.quote: The exam's Illustrative Life Table lists $1000A_x$, $1000\,{}^2\!A_x$ and $\ddot{a}_x$ at $i = 0.06$

requirements.statement: The actuarial present value of a benefit is the expected value of the discounted payment, i.e. the sum over possible payment times of the payment times the discount factor times the probability of that payment.

places.quote: $$\text{EPV} = \sum_{k} \text{CF}_k\, v^{k}\,\Pr(\text{CF}_k \text{ is paid})$$

requirements.statement: The probability of surviving k years from age x is the product of one-year survival probabilities (1 - q) over those years: kp_x = prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(1 - q_{x+j}).

places.quote: Survival probabilities **multiply** across periods: $_{s+t}p_x = {}_{s}p_x \cdot {}_{t}p_{x+s}$

requirements.statement: The probability of failing (dying) in year k+1 is the probability of surviving k years times the one-year failure rate: k|q_x = kp_x * q_{x+k}.

places.quote: $_{t|}q_x = {}_{t}p_x \cdot q_{x+t}$ is the probability of dying in the year *after* surviving $t$ years (a deferred death probability)

requirements.statement: The APV of a term insurance paying a benefit at the end of the year of death is the benefit times the sum over years k=1..N of v^k * (k-1)p_x * q_{x+k-1}, with v = 1/(1+i).

The APV of a term benefit increases with the term length, since each added year contributes a nonnegative amount; so the largest term with APV below a threshold is found by accumulating yearly terms until the threshold is exceeded.
In the acceptance-rejection method, generate a proposal Y from density g and an independent uniform U on (0,1), accept Y (set X = Y) if U ≤ f(Y)/(c·g(Y)), and otherwise repeat.

places.quote: (1) generate $Y$ from $g$; (2) generate $U$ from a [[Uniform Continuous Distribution|Uniform]]$(0,1)$ distribution, independent of $Y$; (3) if $U \leq f(Y)/\bigl(c\,g(Y)\bigr)$, accept and set $X = Y$, otherwise return to step 1.

requirements.statement: The rejection constant c is the maximum over the support of f(x)/g(x), so that f(x) ≤ c·g(x) for all x.

places.quote: The smallest valid constant, $c = \max_x f(x)/g(x)$, is therefore the best one
$$c \geq \max_x \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}$$

requirements.statement: To find the maximum of a density (or ratio f/g) on an interval, set its derivative equal to zero, solve for the critical point, and evaluate the function there.
requirements.concept: Optimization of a Function by Derivatives

places.quote: $c$ is the maximum of the density, $c = \max_x f(x)$, found by setting $f'(x) = 0$.
(a) Maximise $f$: $f'(x) = 20(1-x)^2(1 - 4x) = 0$ gives $x = \frac{1}{4}$, so

requirements.statement: When the proposal density g is uniform on (0,1), g(x) = 1, so the ratio f/g equals f and c equals the maximum of f.

places.quote: **With $g$ uniform on $(0, 1)$:** $g(x) = 1$, so $c$ is the maximum of the density, $c = \max_x f(x)$, found by setting $f'(x) = 0$. The acceptance test is $U \leq f(Y)/c$.

requirements.statement: A policy limit right-censors the loss data: a payment equal to the limit indicates only that the underlying loss was at least the limit, while payments below the limit are exact loss values.

places.quote: A limit right-censors the loss. The variable $X \wedge u$ has a point mass of $S(u)$ at $u$, and a claim recorded at the limit says only that the loss was at least $u$, which is why such a claim enters a likelihood as $S(u)$
A loss at or above the maximum covered loss is recorded only as "at least $u$", so it contributes $S(u)$.

requirements.statement: The likelihood for censored data is the product of the density at each exact observation and the survival function at each censored observation; maximize it (typically via the log-likelihood) to get the MLE.

places.quote: **[[Censoring]]**: observation is known to exceed some value $c$; contribute $P(X > c \mid \theta) = S(c \mid \theta)$ to the likelihood
$$L(\theta) = f(2|\theta)\cdot f(3|\theta)\cdot S(4|\theta) = \frac{1}{\theta}e^{-2/\theta}\cdot\frac{1}{\theta}e^{-3/\theta}\cdot e^{-4/\theta} = \frac{1}{\theta^2}e^{-9/\theta}$$
$$L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \frac{f(x_i \mid \theta)^{\delta_i}\; S(x_i \mid \theta)^{1-\delta_i}}{S(d_i \mid \theta)}$$

requirements.statement: For an exponential distribution with right-censored data, the MLE of the mean is the sum of all observed values (censored ones at their censoring point) divided by the number of uncensored observations.

places.quote: Taking the log and differentiating: $\ell(\theta) = -2\ln\theta - 9/\theta$; $\ell'(\theta) = -2/\theta + 9/\theta^2 = 0$ gives $\hat{\theta} = 9/2 = 4.5$.

For an [[Exponential Distribution|exponential]] model with any mix of truncation and right censoring, $\hat\theta = \dfrac{\sum_i (x_i - d_i)}{\text{number of exact observations}}$, summing over *all* observations, censored ones included.

requirements.statement: The Fisher information of a parameter is the expected value of the negative second derivative of the log-density (log-likelihood) with respect to that parameter, I(θ) = -E[∂² ln f(X;θ)/∂θ²], equivalently the variance of the score.

places.quote: $$I(\theta) = E\!\left[\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\ln f(X\mid\theta)\right)^{2}\right] = -E\!\left[\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\theta^{2}}\ln f(X\mid\theta)\right]$$

requirements.statement: To compute Fisher information for a single observation, take the log of the density, differentiate twice with respect to the parameter, then take the negative expectation over the random variable.

places.quote: $$\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\lambda^2}\ln f = -\frac{x}{\lambda^2} \ \Longrightarrow\ I(\lambda) = -E\!\left[-\frac{X}{\lambda^2}\right] = \frac{\lambda}{\lambda^2} = \frac{1}{\lambda}$$

requirements.statement: For a normal distribution with known variance σ², the Fisher information for the mean μ from one observation is 1/σ², since the second derivative of the log-density with respect to μ is the constant -1/σ².
The expectation of a constant is the constant itself, so when the second derivative of the log-density does not depend on x, no integration is needed to take the expectation.
An estimator is consistent if it converges in probability to the true parameter value as the sample size n goes to infinity.

places.quote: An estimator $\hat{\theta}_n$ is **consistent** for $\theta$ if it converges in probability to the true parameter value as the sample size grows without bound

requirements.statement: An estimator whose bias and variance both go to zero as n goes to infinity is consistent (asymptotically unbiased with vanishing variance implies convergence in probability).

places.quote: if $\text{Bias}(\hat{\theta}_n) \to 0$ and $\text{Var}(\hat{\theta}_n) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$, then $\hat{\theta}_n$ is consistent

requirements.statement: For a random sample of size n from Uniform(0, θ), the sample maximum has expected value nθ/(n+1).

places.quote: Use $E[X_{(n)}] = \frac{n\theta}{n+1}$ and $\text{Var}(X_{(n)}) = \frac{n\theta^2}{(n+1)^2(n+2)}$.
the MLE is $\hat\theta = X_{(n)}$ with $E[X_{(n)}] = \frac{n}{n+1}\theta$

requirements.statement: For a random sample of size n from Uniform(0, θ), the sample maximum has variance nθ²/((n+1)²(n+2)).

places.quote: Use $E[X_{(n)}] = \frac{n\theta}{n+1}$ and $\text{Var}(X_{(n)}) = \frac{n\theta^2}{(n+1)^2(n+2)}$.

requirements.statement: The sample maximum of a Uniform(0, θ) sample is a biased but asymptotically unbiased estimator of θ; multiplying or dividing it by a factor that grows or shrinks with n destroys convergence to θ.

places.quote: The MLE understates $\theta$, which makes sense — the largest observation can never exceed the true maximum. Rescaling removes it:
so $X_{(n)} \xrightarrow{p} \theta$ and the sample maximum is consistent — even though it is biased low for every $n$

requirements.statement: For a normal sample of size n with unbiased sample variance s^2, the statistic (n-1)s^2/sigma_0^2 follows a chi-square distribution with n-1 degrees of freedom under H0: sigma^2 = sigma_0^2.
requirements.concept: Chi-Square Test for a Normal Variance

places.quote: Use $\chi^2 = (n-1)S^2/\sigma_0^2$ against $\chi^2_{\alpha,\,n-1}$.
for a sample of size $n$ from $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ with [[Sample Variance|sample variance]] $S^2$, $(n - 1)S^2/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2(n - 1)$.

requirements.statement: For a lower-tailed variance test (H1: sigma^2 < sigma_0^2), reject H0 when the chi-square statistic is smaller than the lower-tail critical value, i.e. the chi-square percentile at level alpha from the left.
requirements.concept: Chi-Square Test for a Normal Variance

places.quote: a lower-tailed test rejects when $T \le c$ with $P(T \le c \mid H_0) = \alpha$
The CAS MAS-I table** gives *lower-tail* areas for $n = 1$ to 50: the entry in column $p$ is the value $c$ with $P(V \leq c) = p$

requirements.statement: Read critical values from a chi-square table with n-1 degrees of freedom and compare the statistic to critical values at several significance levels to determine the smallest level at which H0 is rejected.
requirements.concept: Hypothesis Testing Critical Values and Significance Level

places.quote: Compare with $\chi^2(3)$. The $df = 3$ row gives $7.81$ in the $0.950$ column and $9.35$ in the $0.975$ column.

requirements.statement: The likelihood ratio statistic Λ is the ratio of the maximized likelihood under the null hypothesis to the maximized likelihood under the full (unrestricted) parameter space, and it lies between 0 and 1.

places.quote: $$\Lambda = \frac{\sup_{\theta \in \Theta_0} L(\theta)}{\sup_{\theta \in \Theta} L(\theta)}$$

requirements.statement: For large samples, -2 ln Λ is approximately chi-squared distributed under the null hypothesis (Wilks' theorem).

places.quote: $$-2\ln\Lambda = 2\left[\ell(\hat\theta) - \ell(\hat\theta_0)\right] \ \dot\sim\ \chi^2_{r}$$
for nested models with $p_1 < p_2$ parameters, $-2\ln\lambda = 2(\ell_2 - \ell_1)$ is approximately $\chi^2(p_2 - p_1)$ in large samples.

requirements.statement: The degrees of freedom of the chi-squared approximation equal the number of free parameters in the full model minus the number of free parameters under the null hypothesis (here, one parameter fixed gives 1 degree of freedom).

places.quote: $r$ is the number of **restrictions** — the difference in free parameters between the full and reduced models — and the $\chi^2$ approximation is asymptotic (Wilks' theorem)

requirements.statement: Reject the null hypothesis in a likelihood ratio test when -2 ln Λ exceeds the chi-squared critical value at the (1 - significance level) percentile; so the rejection region corresponds to small Λ, and the largest Λ that leads to rejection is exp(-critical value / 2).

places.quote: Reject $H_0$ (the reduced model) when $-2\ln\Lambda$ exceeds the upper-$\alpha$ point of $\chi^2_r$
a gap above $3.84/2 = 1.92$ would have rejected.

requirements.statement: For a Poisson process, conditional on n events occurring in [0, t], the number of events in a subinterval [0, s] with s < t is Binomial with n trials and success probability s/t.
The binomial probability of exactly k successes in n trials with success probability p is C(n,k) p^k (1-p)^(n-k).

places.quote: $$P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k}$$

requirements.statement: Given the total number of events in a Poisson process over an interval, the conditional probability of events in a subinterval does not depend on the rate lambda.
A Type I error is rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true, and its probability is computed by evaluating the rejection-region probability under the null hypothesis parameter value.

places.quote: A **Type I Error** occurs when a [[Hypothesis Testing|hypothesis test]] incorrectly **rejects a true null hypothesis** $H_0$.
The **critical region** is constructed so that $P(\text{test statistic in critical region} \mid H_0) = \alpha$

requirements.statement: A gamma distribution with shape alpha and scale theta has mean alpha*theta and variance alpha*theta^2.

places.quote: $E[X] = \alpha\theta$, $\text{Var}(X) = \alpha\theta^2$, and coefficient of variation $CV = 1/\sqrt{\alpha}$

requirements.statement: By the central limit theorem, the sample mean of n independent identically distributed observations is approximately normal with mean mu and standard deviation sigma/sqrt(n).

places.quote: By the [[Central Limit Theorem]], $\bar{X}$ is approximately $N(\mu, \sigma^2/n)$ for large $n$ whatever the population shape
$$\frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}} \xrightarrow{d} N(0, 1)$$

requirements.statement: Standardize the sample mean by subtracting the mean and dividing by sigma/sqrt(n), then use standard normal tail probabilities to compute the probability of exceeding a cutoff.

places.quote: $$P(\bar{X} \le x) \approx \Phi\!\left(\frac{x - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}\right)$$

requirements.statement: The standard normal critical value with upper-tail probability 0.025 is 1.96, so a tail probability below 0.025 requires the z-cutoff to exceed 1.96.
Because sample size must be a whole number, solve the inequality for n and take the smallest integer satisfying it.

requirements.statement: A chi-square test of independence tests whether two categorical variables in a contingency table are independent, with the null hypothesis that the row and column classifications are independent.

places.quote: The same statistic on a $k \times m$ contingency table, with $E_{ij} = (\text{row } i \text{ total})(\text{column } j \text{ total})/n$, tests whether two classifications are independent, on $(k-1)(m-1)$ degrees of freedom.

requirements.statement: Under independence, the expected count for each cell of a contingency table equals (row total) times (column total) divided by the grand total.

places.quote: $E_{ij} = (\text{row } i \text{ total})(\text{column } j \text{ total})/n$
Expected counts are row total × column total ÷ $600$: $15$, $85$, $75$ and $425$.

requirements.statement: The chi-square statistic is the sum over all cells of (observed - expected)^2 divided by expected.

places.quote: Pearson's $X^2 = \sum (y_{ij} - \hat\mu_{ij})^2/\hat\mu_{ij}$ is the traditional alternative.

requirements.statement: For independent normal samples with sample variances s1^2 and s2^2 of sizes n1 and n2, under H0: sigma1^2 = sigma2^2 the ratio s1^2/s2^2 follows an F distribution with (n1-1, n2-1) degrees of freedom.

places.quote: for independent normal samples of sizes $n_X$ and $n_Y$, $\dfrac{S_X^2/\sigma_X^2}{S_Y^2/\sigma_Y^2} \sim F(n_X - 1,\ n_Y - 1)$
Under $H_0$, $s_A^2/s_B^2 \sim F(10, 8)$, and the observed ratio is $2.4/0.8 = 3.0$.

requirements.statement: The maximum of several random variables is less than a value x exactly when every one of the variables is less than x.

places.quote: The minimum is $X_{(1)}$ and the maximum is $X_{(n)}$.

requirements.statement: For independent random variables, the probability that all of them satisfy their events equals the product of the individual probabilities.

places.quote: $$P\bigl(X_{(n)} \le x\bigr) = F_1(x)\,F_2(x)\cdots F_n(x)$$
